The fifth is a boy who says his mother goes in on Thursdays and comes out with the shopping already done.

choices.text: Follow the boy home and talk to his mother.

c.text:
Bills, circulars, and {many} letters in the same hand, all addressed to the shop and all signed by the shopkeeper, posted from further and further away over {two years|three years|eighteen months}.
The last has a bank draft in it, made out to the bearer, and a line asking that the shutters be kept down.

a1.text:
{few} customers in the hour and each of them asks for something the party would not have believed was in the stock, and each time the party finds it {exactly|precisely} where they reach.
The shopkeeper comes back at the hour, pays the hour's wage {properly|correctly}, and asks nothing else.

a2.text: The stock does not object. The street does. Everybody on it turns round {at once|all at the same time|together}, and the piece of pavement {nobody|no one} walks on is now behind the party.

b1.text:
Thursday, and the shutters are up, and inside it is an ordinary shop full of ordinary people, and the shopkeeper is glad to be asked because {nobody|no one} ever asks.
{What is kept in the back room|Whatever it is they keep in the back room} is given to the party outright, on the condition that they take it a long way from here.

b2.text:
She sits the party down, feeds them, and explains the arrangement the street has with the shop in {about|something like|roughly} {few} sentences, none of which anybody enjoys.
She also sends them away with the week's shopping, which is more than it should be, and a doctor's kit her husband no longer needs.

n0.text:
In the impound yard at the end of the quay there is one crate under a tarpaulin with {few} different customs seals on it, from {few} countries, none of them cancelled.
The yard man has been paid to leave it and paid again to say who left it.

choices.text: Come back for the crate at night.
Take the paperwork instead of the crate.

a.text:
It came off a ship that is not on the register, was landed by men who spoke the wrong language for the flag, and has been claimed {three times by three consignees|three separate times by three consignees} who each looked at the seals and left without it.
He will look the other way for {an hour|the hour|half an hour}. He will not touch it himself.

b.text: The yard at two {in the morning|first thing|before noon} has {three|four|two} men in it who are not the watchman, working by shuttered lamp, doing to the crate what people do when they intend to take one thing out of a box and leave the box looking untouched.

choices.text: Watch, and take it off them afterwards.

c.text:
{few} manifests, {few} seals, {few} sets of lies, and taken together they describe a route that certain people would very much prefer {nobody|no one} drew on a map.
They buy the map back. They pay well and they pay quickly.

a1.text: {Straw, then lead sheet, then a case with a handle on it|Straw, then sheet lead, then a case with a carrying handle}, and inside the case a single object packed for a journey that was {clearly|plainly} expected to be much longer than a crossing.

a2.text:
{few} men and an hour to get it onto a cart, and {nobody|no one} stops them, and everybody watches.
What is in it is worth the carrying, and the people whose seals are on it will be along in their own time.

b1.text: {They are not dockers and they are armed|They are not dockers, and they are armed} and they {have done this before|have plainly done this before}.

b2.text:
They take one thing out, re-seal the crate {beautifully|perfectly|so well nobody would know}, and are on the quay steps with it when the party steps out of the dark.
They hand it over rather than {lose the hour|lose the hour arguing}. They are professionals, and so, tonight, is everybody.

n0.text:
A shrine at the roadside: a niche, {saint} with the face worn off, a shelf of stubs and coins, and a boot. One boot, good quality, set on the shelf like an offering.
{A hundred|Two hundred|Eighty} paces on there is another shrine. There is a boot on that one too.

choices.text: Walk the road shrine to shrine.
Leave a coin at each and pass on.

a.text:
{Eleven|Nine|Thirteen} shrines in four miles and a boot on every one, all of them left boots, all of them different sizes, none of them older than a year.
At the twelfth there is no boot. {There is a place cleared for one.|A place has been cleared for one.}

choices.text: Put a boot of your own on the shelf.

b.text:
{They come off the shelves easily.|They lift off the shelves without any trouble.} By the third the road behind the party has gone quiet, and by the fifth there is {somebody|someone} walking it a long way back, keeping pace, not gaining.
They are not wearing boots.

choices.text: Keep walking and let them come.

c.text:
{A coin at each and a hand on the stone|A coin at every one of them, and a hand on the stone}, which is what the country people here do without thinking about it.
The road runs well. The weather holds. Nobody's cart throws a wheel this side of the border, and in this country that is worth more than the coins.

a1.text:
{leader}'s own boot on the shelf, which means walking on in one, which is a long {few} miles.
At the end of it, on the last shrine, there is a pair: new, made for that foot, and a purse besides, from {somebody|someone} who evidently keeps {very|remarkably} careful accounts.

a2.text: He comes up the road {at dusk|at last light|as the light goes} carrying the twelfth boot and he is {very|remarkably} tired and he has been doing this {a long time|a good while|longer than anybody says}. He would like to stop. He would like to hand the whole route over.

b1.text:
{many} shrines, backwards, in the dark, at a jog. The last one goes back on its shelf with the walker {lots} paces off, and he stops, and turns round, and goes back the way he came.
{Nobody|No one} in the party ever leaves a road shrine unsaluted again.

b2.text: He does not gain for six miles {and then|then|and after that}, all {at once|at the same time}, he is not behind the party any more.

n0.text:
The tide has left a line up the beach for {two miles|a mile and a half|three miles}, and it is all one wreck: dunnage, a hatch cover, crates, a ship's name board, {and not one splinter of it wet|and not a splinter of it damp}.
Whatever went down went down a long way from here and {a long time|a good while|longer than anybody says} ago.

choices.text: Follow it to whatever is at the end of it.
Report the name board to the harbour office.

a.text:
{few} crates unbroken, a chest, and a locker with a padlock {somebody|someone} has {already|by now} tried and failed to break.
Everything the sea has given up here is dry, and the chest, when it is moved, is not the weight it looks.

choices.text: Take the crates and leave the chest.

b.text:
At the top of the beach, above the tide, above where anything the sea throws could reach, there is a boat {drawn up|hauled up|pulled up out of reach}, and it is the ship's boat off the name board, and it is dry inside.
There are footprints leading out of it and up the dune. {Only one set.|One set, and no others.}

choices.text: Take the boat's gear and go the other way.

c.text:
The name is on the register: lost with all hands, {sixty-one|fifty-nine|seventy-two} years ago, {many} hundred miles from this coast.
The insurers stopped paying on it a lifetime back and the maritime museum has not, and they take the board and the whole account of where it lay.

a1.text: {Ship's papers, a captain's instruments|The ship's papers, the master's instruments}, and under a false bottom the thing the captain was carrying that is {not on any manifest and never was|on no manifest, and never was}.

a2.text:
{Good salvage, hauled clear of the tide|Honest salvage, dragged clear of the water} and carted off before the beachcombers are up: cordage, tinned stores, sailcloth and a barrel of oil that has kept.
The chest is still {sitting|standing} on the sand and the sea has not come back for it.

b1.text: They go over the dune and inland for {a mile and a half|two miles|a mile} and stop at a house that has been empty for years, and the door is open, and whoever walked up from the boat is sitting in the kitchen with {their back to it|their back to the door}.

b2.text:
{Oars, a compass that still swings true|Oars, and a compass that still finds north}, a water breaker and a bag of tools stowed the way a good boatswain stows them.
Walking off the beach the party passes the footprints again, going the other way now, which {nobody|no one} mentions until they are well up the road.

n0.text:
There is a weir here that is on no map and belongs to no mill, {cut stone, well kept|dressed stone, well kept}, and it holds the water back {a foot and a half|two feet|a foot}.
On the still side there is something under the surface with a straight edge, and the fish will not go over it.

choices.text: Wade out to the straight edge.
Open the weir and let the water down.

a.text:
{Chest-deep and cold|Chest-deep, and cold with it}, and it is a roof: tile, ridge, chimney, a whole house standing on its own floor under {three feet|a metre|four feet} of water, and the door in it is shut.
The weir was built to keep the water over this.

choices.text: Go back and leave it under.

b.text:
The sluice gear is greased. {Somebody|Someone} maintains this. The water goes down over an hour and what comes out of it is a street, a green, a well, and around the well the whole village sitting where they sat down.
They have been under the water a {very|remarkably} long time and they are not bones.

choices.text: Shut the sluice and put the water back.

c.text:
Nothing takes for two hours {and then|then|and after that} everything does {at once|all at the same time|together}, and the fish out of the still side are enormous and pale and {perfectly|entirely} good eating, and there is more of them than the party can carry.
The last one out of the water has a ring in its gut, and the ring is warm.

a1.text: It opens outward, and it opens into a kitchen {with air in it, dry, and a lamp burning|with dry air in it and a lamp still burning}, and a table with one place laid, and on the plate the thing this whole weir was built to keep {somebody|someone} from coming and taking.

a2.text:
Back over the weir with nothing, which {is a decision|is its own kind of decision}, and the fish come back over the straight edge as soon as the party is out of the water.
What that was worth is not in the packs. {Everybody knows what they did not do.|Everybody knows exactly what they did not do.}

b1.text: {They are all facing the well|Every one of them is facing the well} and the well is open and the water in the party's boots is going {the wrong way, uphill|uphill, which is the wrong way}, towards it.

b2.text:
The sluice takes both of {leader}'s hands and an hour to close and the water comes back up over the green, the well and the sitting, and stops where it was.
The grease pot is still on the ledge. {Somebody|Someone} has left a purse beside it, which is a wage for an hour's work, paid in full.

n0.text:
There is a marker here that {nobody|no one} in {region} put up: a post, a heap, a cut in a rock face, in the middle of {place} where there is no reason to mark anything.
Something has been left at the foot of it, out of the weather, and it has been left recently.

choices.text: Leave something of your own and go on.

a.text:
It is {a bundle|a wrapped bundle}, tied the way a person ties a thing they expect {somebody|someone} else to untie, and inside it there is food, a length of good rope, and a paper with a direction on it in a hand that has written a great many of these.
The direction is not towards anything the party can see.

choices.text: Go the way the paper says.
Keep the bundle and go your own way.

b.text: It takes {most of a day|the better part of a day|a whole day}, and it is not a person. It comes to the marker {the way a postman comes to a box|the way a postman comes to a letterbox}: with something to leave, and something to collect, and no interest in anybody standing there.

c.text:
{Salt, a coin and a strip of dried meat|Salt, a coin, and dried meat}, set out of the rain under the lee of the marker.
Two days later, well away from here, the party's own stores are heavier than they were, and {nobody|no one} is short of anything for a month.

a1.text: Four hours out, {exactly|precisely} where the paper stops, there is a second marker, and a cache under it, and the cache has been stocked for {somebody|someone} who never came.

a2.text:
{The rope is good and the food is good|The rope is good, and so is the food} and both of them go a long way.
Whatever was walking out to collect that bundle turns and follows the party instead, and it is patient, and it catches up {at dusk|at last light|as the light goes}.

b1.text:
{leader} puts a letter in its hand, and it takes it, and it goes.
What is at the foot of the marker on the way back is the answer, in a hand {nobody|no one} knows, and wrapped around something that has been a long way to get here.

b2.text: It has been walking this route for longer than {region} has had a name, {and it does not stop for people|and it has never once stopped for people}.

n0.text:
{Somebody|Someone} camped here and left in a hurry: a fire dead {about|something like|roughly} a day, a tent still pegged, a pot of food gone cold on the stones and a pack sitting open beside it.
Nothing has been dragged. There is no blood. The boots are still by the tent door.

choices.text: Cast around for the trail out.
Rebuild the fire and stay the night in it.

a.text:
{Two of everything for one person|Everything doubled, for one person}, a journal in {a private shorthand|a shorthand of the writer's own}, and a tin box that has been buried and dug up again more than once.
The last page of the journal is a drawing of this exact ground, with a cross on the spot where the party is standing.

b.text:
{The trail out is barefoot|Whoever walked out went barefoot} and it goes away from the road, away from water, and away from every direction a lost person walks.
It is also not one set of prints all the way. About {two hundred|three hundred|a hundred and fifty} paces out it becomes two, then {few}.

choices.text: Go back to the camp and wait for the owner.

c.text:
The fire takes, the food is good, and the tent is a better one than the party owns.
{Nobody|No one} comes back for it {in the night|overnight}. In the morning everything is {exactly|precisely} where it was, and there is one more pair of boots by the door than there was {at dusk|at last light|as the light goes}.

a1.text: {Eighteen inches|Two feet|A foot and a half} down, wrapped in waxed cloth, is what the camper had been carrying around long enough to bury it every night: worth burying, and worth {leaving a tent behind|abandoning a tent} to get away from.

a2.text:
It goes in the pack and it stays shut, all the way out, and the party gets {a fortnight|a week|a month} of clean sleep out of not knowing.
The collector who buys it does not open it either, which {tells everybody something|tells the party something}.

b1.text: It ends in a hollow {a mile and a half|two miles|a mile} out where {a great deal|a good deal|rather a lot} of walking has been done in a small circle, and whatever finished walking there is still in the hollow.

b2.text:
They come in {at dusk|at last light|as the light goes} on their own feet, alive, filthy, and {enormously relieved|so relieved they cannot speak} to find anyone at all in their camp.
They pay for the company in the only coin they have left, which is the kit they can now afford to leave behind.

n0.text:
The bowling alley is open, lit, and playing {radio} over the tannoy to nine empty lanes and one that is not.
On lane one, {stranger} is bowling alone against a scorecard {already|by now} filled in for an opponent who has not arrived, and losing to it. {leader} is noticed before the door has shut.

choices.text: Ask who the scorecard belongs to.
Look at the back of the building instead.

a.text:
The wager is the alley: a house game against the party, best of one, and the deeds are in the till in an envelope with {payment} clipped to it.
The alternative offered, with no particular hope, is that the party bowls badly {on purpose|deliberately} and takes {coin} for the trouble.

b.text:
The card is in a hand {nobody|no one} in the building recognises, and it has been filled in ahead of the game: every frame, both players, right down to frame ten.
The scores it predicts for the house are {exactly|precisely} the scores the house has bowled tonight. The other column is still to happen.

choices.text: Take the card and leave the alley to it.

c.text:
Behind the alley, the pinsetter machinery has been serviced by {somebody|someone} who understood it far better than the manual did, and there are {relicWord}s of parts stacked under a tarpaulin, all of them stamped with a mark that is not a manufacturer's.
{One crate is unopened|One of them has never been opened}, addressed here, and paid for by an office that does not exist at the address on the docket.

a1.text: The lane is oiled the way a lane is oiled when {somebody|someone} wants a specific result, and the house has bowled it for {lots} years.

a2.text:
The money is real, the loss is convincing, and the alley stays in the family it has been in since before the roof was on.
The party is fed, paid, and told, {twice|two separate times}, {to come back and never to come back|to come back, and never to come back}.

b1.text:
Bowling {somebody|someone} else's frames is not difficult. Bowling them {exactly|precisely}, ball for ball, with the card face down on the bench, is.
By frame nine the alley has gone quiet in a way a building with a tannoy on should not manage.

b2.text:
The card goes in a pocket, the alley goes back to losing to it, and two streets away the card is still {warm|warm to the hand}.
A Foundation clerk buys it off the party at the tram stop for {coin}, writes a receipt, and asks them not to describe the handwriting to anybody.

e_city_checkpoint.title: {The Publication Order|Checkpoint on {street}|Everything You Are Carrying}

n0.text:
The Foundation has put {a trestle table|a folding table|a table on trestles} across the pavement and two archivists behind it, and everyone going past is having the messages on their phone read out, transcribed, and published.
{The queue is patient.|The queue is patient about it.} The third man in it is sweating, and it is not warm.

choices.text: Queue up and hand the phone over.
Ask the sweating man what is on his.
Walk round the block and come at the table from behind.

a.text:
The archivist reads out everything on {leader}'s handset in a level voice to a street that is pretending not to listen, and thanks the party for their contribution to the record.
She also mentions, filing it, that the Foundation is paying for anything the record does not {already|by now} hold.

choices.text: Sell them something they do not have.
Ask instead what the table is really here for.

b.text:
What is on his phone is {paper}, photographed, from an office of the Collective, and it names {few} people and a price for each.
He would very much like it not to be published, and he is not able to say so out loud this close to the table.

choices.text: Get him out of the queue.
Take the phone to the table yourself.

c.text:
Behind the table there is a van, and in the van there is the day's take: every message from every phone on this street, on tape, catalogued, and nothing on any of the labels about publishing any of it.
The clerk in the van is asleep. The manifest is not locked. {Somebody|Someone} has been keeping a second copy, and the second copy is where the money is.

a1.text:
What the record does not hold, it turns out, is most of where the party has actually been, and the archivists pay {by the entry|by the item|per entry} without haggling once.
The receipt is stamped by an office {three ranks|four ranks|several ranks} above a pavement table.

a2.text:
The table is here because something was published {last week|the week before|on Friday} that should not have been, and the Foundation is working backwards through every handset on the street to find out who published it.
The archivist says this {plainly|flatly}, which is the Foundation all over, and gives the party the address of the office that will pay them for finding it first.

b1.text:
Getting a man out of a Foundation queue takes {about|something like|roughly} ninety seconds of {somebody|someone} else being much more interesting than he is, and {leader} is happy to be that.
He pays in {payment}, and the {few} names on the photographs go on living the rest of the week.

b2.text:
The archivists publish it within the hour, on the street, out loud, and {by evening|by dark|by nightfall} it is in the record for good and {few} people are safer than they were and one office is not.
The Collective takes the loss the way the Collective takes losses, which is to say it writes the party's names down.

e_city_hall.title: {The Table in the Back|Nine Ball, Two Rules|The Hall on {street}}

n0.text:
The pool hall has {smell} and one table lit at the back where four men are watching a fifth line up a shot he has been lining up for some minutes.
House rules are on a card by the door. There are two of them, and the second is that {nobody|no one} plays the man in the corner.

choices.text: Play the man in the corner.
Play the table everybody else is playing.

a.text:
He racks {without being asked|unprompted|before anybody asks} and lets {leader} break, and the {few} men who were watching the other table stop watching the other table.
What he is playing for, he says, is a debt he is carrying for {somebody|someone} else. If he loses it, it is the party's to carry.

choices.text: Refuse the stake and play for money.

b.text:
The regular table is a hustle and everybody in the room including the hustler assumes the party knows it, so the game is played honestly out of sheer politeness and the money moves around the table {twice|two separate times}.
By closing, {leader} has been dealt in on a delivery going out on Thursday and told which door to knock on.

c.text:
The rule exists because the man in the corner won a table off the hall in 1994 and has been waiting since for {somebody|someone} to win it back, and the hall would rather {nobody|no one} did, because of what he put up against it.
The hall gives the party {coin} to leave it alone, which they have not had to do in {many} years.

a1.text: He plays {like a man who learned|like somebody who learned the game} in a room where losing cost more than money, and he has not lost since he {stopped being able to afford to|could no longer afford to}.

a2.text:
Money he can lose, and does, {cheerfully|happily}, {few} times, and buys the party {drink} with what is left.
The debt stays his. He seems relieved and says so once {and then|then|and after that} not again.

e_city_eris.title: {The Woman on the Last Tram|Court Adjourned|Two Stops Past the Depot}

n0.text:
The last tram out of the centre has {eris} on it, alone, in a carriage that has {already|by now} been swept for the night, and the driver has not asked her for a fare.
When {leader} sits down she does not look up from the paperwork she is not reading. "{Somebody|Someone} in this city committed a crime today," she says, "and I am putting it off."

choices.text: Ask her what the crime was.
Ask why she is putting it off.
Get off at the next stop.

a.text:
The crime was that a man in {country} sold a bottle of water that was not water and a child drank it and was ill for a week and is now well.
{The file wants a judicial ghost sent after him.|The file calls for a judicial ghost.} She says the sentence and the crime do not resemble each other in any way she can defend, and she is the last authority anywhere on what she can defend.

choices.text: Tell her the sentence is wrong.
Tell her the law is the law.

b.text:
Because the work is {billions of trials wide and one woman deep|a billion trials wide and one woman deep}, she says, and because the last time she took an evening off, an entire dimension {used it to reorganise itself|took the opportunity to reorganise itself}.
"And," she adds, folding the file into a shape it will not come out of, "because I have not been on a tram since a man I knew drove one for a bet."

choices.text: Ride to the end of the line with her.

c.text:
Getting off is allowed. She waves the party off with the folded file, and the tram goes on with its one passenger.
In the morning there is {coin} in {leader}'s pocket that {nobody|no one} put there, and every clock on the street is agreed on a time that is {few} minutes wrong.

a1.text:
She listens all the way to the depot, argues for two stops, {and then|then|and after that} throws the file out of the window of a moving tram, which is a legal act because she is the one doing it.
The man in {country} will never know. She says the party will have to be the ones who know instead, and that this is the price and it is not a small one.

a2.text:
"Yes," she says. "It is. That is the entire problem, and you are the fourth person this century to say it to me like it settles something."
{The ghost goes out that night.|The ghost goes out the same night.} The party feels it pass on the way to the depot, moving in a straight line through walls, {patient as a bailiff|as patient as a bailiff}.

b1.text:
The end of the line is a turning circle, a shed, and a man with a flask who has worked nights for {lots} years and does not ask who she is.
She buys the round out of a purse with no money in it, and by the time the tram turns round the evening has stopped being about the tram.

b2.text:
She does not name him. She describes a camper, a road that runs through three Americas, and a way of opening a safe that involves asking the safe nicely and meaning it.
Then she stops, in the middle of the sentence, and gives {leader} {payment} for listening, which is her way of ending a conversation she started.

e_village_bell.title: {The Bell That Rings Itself|Forty Houses and a Rope|The Wrong Hours}

n0.text:
The village bell rings at seventeen minutes past, every hour, and has done since {timeAgo}, and the rope in the tower is tied off and dusty.
{Nobody|No one} has taken the bell down because {rumour}, and because the last two people who went up the tower came down agreeing about something and would not say what.

choices.text: Sit in the square and time it {properly|correctly}.

a.text:
{The bell chamber is swept|The bell chamber has been swept}, and the bell is warm, and the beam it hangs from is newer than the tower by {six hundred|five hundred|seven hundred} years.
Something has been wedged into the crown of the bell and mortared over, and the mortar is not old.

choices.text: Leave it and mortar it back.

b.text:
Timed {properly|correctly}, it is not seventeen minutes past. It is seventeen minutes before, of an hour that is not going to happen, and every clock in the village is set to the bell.
The village is a quarter of an hour ahead of {country} and has been for years, and {nobody|no one} has ever been late for anything.

c.text:
The priest is eighty, unbothered, and has been ringing an unrung bell for a congregation of {lots} for longer than most of them have been alive.
He gives the party {food}, the parish register with a page cut out of it, and directions to the only house that keeps its clocks on {country} time.

a1.text:
What is mortared into the crown is a hand's length of metal that rings on its own note when the bell rings, and has been carrying the bell for a century rather than the other way about.
Cut out, the bell goes quiet, and the whole village comes {out into the square|into the square} to hear it not happen.

a2.text:
Mortared back, the bell rings the seventeen minutes as it has always done, and the village goes on being a quarter hour ahead of everybody in {country}.
The priest, who knew {exactly|precisely} what was up there, has {payment} waiting at the bottom of the ladder and does not ask what was decided.

c1.text:
The house on {country} time belongs to a widow who will not have the bell in her kitchen and has not left the village in nine years because outside it she is late for everything, always, by {exactly|precisely} a quarter of an hour.
She gives the party the clock. It is heavier than a clock, and it does not tick so much as wait.

c2.text:
The cut page is in the back of the register, folded, and it records {few} burials in one week {timeAgo} with the same cause written {few} times in a hand that pressed hard enough to go through.
The cause is not an illness. It is a time of day.

e_village_loop.title: {Every Day Is Tuesday|The Village in the Bubble|Eighty Going Out}

n0.text:
The village is having a good Tuesday. The bread is fresh, the washing is out, {animal} is asleep in the road, and the man at the pump says, {without being asked|unprompted|before anybody asks}, that {loopTalk}.
They have known for {many} years. The bubble is {about|something like|roughly} two miles across and the road out is the one the party walked in on.

choices.text: Ask who else is inside with them.

a.text:
They live well. Nothing spoils, nothing runs out, {nobody|no one} sickens, and any injury is gone by morning as long as the injured party was standing still when it happened.
The diary is kept in the pub in {many} volumes, and the entries got shorter each year until they stopped, {and then|then|and after that} {somebody|someone} started them again last spring.

choices.text: Read the volume that starts again.

b.text:
What they want is a pigeon loft, because the pigeons are the only post that crosses the edge, and theirs blew down and {nobody|no one} inside can build one that lasts past midnight because midnight puts it back where it was.
They want it built outside the edge and carried in whole, which is {a morning's work|half a day's work} and two miles of carrying.

c.text:
Inside with them is a Collective agent who came to sell them the way out and has been here {few} years, which is to say one {very|remarkably} long Tuesday.
He is immune to the reset, having spent a life above eighty, and he has been going through the village's houses {every day|day in and day out} and putting everything back before midnight.

choices.text: Take him out of the village.

a1.text:
The new entries are in a child's hand and they are a list of everything that is different each day, which for {many} years was nothing and is now three or {few} things.
The last page has {many} differences on it, and the bubble is coming apart, and the village does not know.

a2.text:
The girl who started it again is nine, has been nine for {many} years, and is the only one in the village who never stopped noticing.
She hands over the volume without ceremony and asks for nothing, {and then|then|and after that} asks for {tool}, and gets it.

c1.text:
Getting him out means getting him above eighty on a road that never gets above {lots}, downhill, on a cart, with the whole village pushing and the edge of the bubble coming up fast.
He goes over the edge shouting something about a contract. What he leaves behind, {few} years of it, is under the floor of the room he rented.

c2.text:
{What he is selling is genuine|What he is selling is the real thing}: an engine, calibrated, that will take a cart over the edge, and a price that would take the village {three generations|four generations|a century} to pay if the village had generations.
He sells the party the calibration alone, cash, and throws in the sentence that the Collective would rather they did not carry it out of here.

e_village_witch.title: {The Woman at the End of the Lane|Not a Witch, Says the Village|The Poultice}

n0.text:
There is a woman at the end of the lane who is not a witch, the village says, {unprompted|without being asked}, {few} times, before anybody has asked.
What she is, is the person the village goes to at night with {misfortune}, and she has never once turned anybody away, and none of them will be seen going.

choices.text: Ask the village what they actually think.

a.text:
She is younger than the story, works out of a kitchen that smells of {smell}, and is quite open about the fact that most of what she does is a poultice, patience, and knowing everybody's family for three generations.
The rest of it is not a poultice. She shows {leader} the rest of it {without being asked|unprompted|before anybody asks}, which is either trust or exhaustion.

choices.text: Ask her to teach the trick of it.
Warn her that showing people is how they find you.

b.text:
What the village actually thinks, once the pub is three deep and {nobody|no one} is being overheard, is that she has kept {few} children alive that the county hospital would not have, and that if anybody official ever asks, she is a herbalist.
They have rehearsed this. They have rehearsed it as a village, out loud, more than once.

c.text:
After dark the lane is busy. {many} people in three hours, none of them acknowledging any of the others, and one of them a man in a good coat who came out by car and left the car a field away.
The man in the good coat is not sick, and he was inside for {few} minutes, and he wrote something down before he drove off.

a1.text:
It cannot be taught in an evening, and she says so, and teaches what can be: {the reading of a line under a floor|how to read a line under a floor}, the four questions, and why the second one is the one that matters.
She sends the party off with a book that is not a grimoire and a warning about the ones that are.

a2.text:
She has been told before. She points out that the alternative is a village that buries its children {properly|correctly} and on time, and offers {leader} {drink}, and the conversation is over.
What she gives the party at the door is worth more than the argument was.

c1.text:
The car goes {lots} miles to an office with no plate on the door, and what the man in the good coat wrote down goes into a file with {many} names in it, of which hers is the newest.
The file is not hard to take. What is hard is deciding, in a corridor, with the light on a timer, whether taking it helps her or simply moves the date.

c2.text:
She goes white, {and then|then|and after that} she goes practical, and by first light the kitchen is a kitchen and the rest of it is under a hedge two fields away in a biscuit tin.
She gives the party the tin to carry out of the county, because a stranger carrying it is the only version of this where {nobody|no one} local is holding anything.

e_village_fair.title: {The Fair on the Green|Three Shots a Go|The Shooting Gallery}

n0.text:
The village has a fair up on the green: {few} stalls, {food}, {sound}, and a shooting gallery run by a man who has been running it since {timeAgo}.
The top prize has never been won. It is on the shelf in a glass case, and the case is dusty and the prize is not.

choices.text: Look at the sights on the rifles.

a.text:
{Three shots, a penny each|Three shots for a penny each|Three shots, a penny a go}, and the man does not put his hand anywhere near the sights while the party watches.
He does say, conversationally, that the last person to come close was in {a great hurry|a considerable hurry} afterwards.

b.text:
The prize came off a dead man on this green {timeAgo}, and the man who runs the gallery has been trying to give it away for a decade to {somebody|someone} who earns it, because giving it away any other way did not work and he has tried.
He has tried {few} times. He will describe two of them.

choices.text: Just take it off the shelf.

c.text:
The sights are true, which for a fairground rifle is {an act of open hostility|an act of open aggression}, and the barrels have been re-crowned by {somebody|someone} who cared.
The gallery is not the fiddle. The fiddle is that the pellets are heavier than they look, and the party is welcome to a tin of them.

b1.text:
It comes off the shelf easily, and the fair goes on, and {about|something like|roughly} two miles down the road out of the village it becomes clear what the other {few} takers had in common.
They were all carrying it when it happened, and so is the party.

b2.text: {Properly means the full card|Doing it properly means the full card}, in front of the village, with the man watching the party's hands {rather than the targets|and not the targets}.

e_village_truckers.title: {The Convoy in the Yard|Load and Two Pigeons|Nights on the Encompassing Road}

n0.text:
Three lorries are parked in the yard behind the village pub, nose out, engines warm, and the drivers are inside arguing about a road they all agree is closed.
On the table between them is {paper} and a pigeon in a shoebox, and they stop talking when {leader} comes in, {and then|then|and after that} start again, louder, which is the Society's way of saying sit down.

choices.text: Offer to ride out with them.

a.text:
The road is closed because the bubble on it has grown, and the load is medicine, and the people it is for are inside the bubble and have been reordering it {every day|day in and day out} for a month without knowing it.
The argument is whether to run the edge at eighty with a full trailer, which two of them will not do, or go round, which takes {nine days|nine whole days} the load does not have.

choices.text: Ride the edge with the one who will.

b.text:
Riding out with a Society convoy means keeping your mouth shut at the first checkpoint and open at the second, and knowing which is which, and the party is told which by {a man who does not repeat himself|somebody who will not say it twice}.
By the county line they are dealt in {properly|correctly} and told what the flashing pattern on the last lorry means.

c.text:
The pigeon is post, the only post that crosses an edge, and there is a stick of memory tied to its leg the size of a fingernail.
What is on it is nine months of what a bubbled village has been living, recorded by {somebody|someone} inside it who has been recording {carefully|with care}. The Foundation would pay well. So would the Collective, for different reasons.

a1.text:
Eighty out of a yard, through a village, and at the edge the cab goes quiet the way a room goes quiet, {and then|then|and after that} it is Tuesday everywhere and the load is inside.
Getting out again is the same trick backwards, with a trailer twelve tons lighter and a village standing in the road {to wave|waving}.

a2.text:
The third way is to take the load in on foot, in relays, two miles each way, with the whole yard carrying and the drivers carrying most of it.
It takes {a night|the whole night|one night}. Nothing goes above walking pace and nothing needs to, and {at dawn|at first light} the Society owes the party a debt it writes down in the place it writes those.

e_road_hitch.title: {The Hitch-hiker|Thumb Out on the {country} Road|Somebody Waiting at the Junction}

n0.text:
There is {eris} standing at the junction with her thumb out, in {weather}, on a road where nothing has passed in an hour.
She is not wet. The verge around her is, and she is not, and she says the party is later than she had them down for.

choices.text: Ask how far she is going.
Ask how long she has been waiting.

a.text:
As far as anybody is going, she says, and produces a map of {country} with every road on it drawn in and one road drawn in that is not on any other map.
That road, she says, comes out {somewhere it should not|somewhere no road should}, and she has never taken it {with company|in company}.

choices.text: Take the road that is not on the map.
Keep to the road that is.

b.text:
"Since the junction," she says, which is not an answer about time, {and then|then|and after that}, because {leader} waits her out: "There is a bubble {few} miles up. I have been standing outside it enjoying the concept of afternoon."
She adds that there is a driver inside it who has been having the same accident {every day|day in and day out} since {timeAgo}, and that this is not her doing and she can prove it, which is not a thing she often has to say.

choices.text: Go and get the driver out.
Ask her to fix it herself.

c.text:
Walking past is allowed and she does not comment, and the road goes on being a road for four miles.
At the fifth mile there is a junction, and it is the same junction, and there is {nobody|no one} standing at it, and {leader} finds {coin} in a pocket that was empty.

a1.text:
The turn-off is a farm track for a hundred yards {and then|then|and after that} it is not a farm track, and the hedges on either side are hedges from {few} different countries and one that is not a country.
Where it comes out is a lay-by in the dark with a van in it, a kettle on, and a conversation that goes on until the light comes up.

a2.text:
The ordinary road is ordinary for six miles {and then|then|and after that} goes past a wreck that has been cleared and re-cleared, and she asks to be let out there without explaining.
What she leaves on the seat is not payment. It is the sort of thing that is left {deliberately|on purpose}, and it is worth {a great deal|a good deal|rather a lot}.

b1.text:
{few} miles up there is a lorry on its side that is not on its side, a driver who has climbed out of it {many} thousand times, and an edge you can feel on your teeth.
Getting him out means getting him to eighty going outward, and the only thing on the road that will do eighty is the thing that keeps crashing.

b2.text:
She could. She says so. She also says that the last {few} times she reached into a bubble to be kind about it, the bubble stopped being a bubble and started being a hole, and one of those is still on the map as a lake.
Instead she walks up the road with the party as far as the edge, says something to it that is not in a language, and the driver walks out on his own two feet {at dusk|at last light|as the light goes}.

e_road_convoy.title: {The Second Lorry|Convoy at the County Line|Hazards Going}

n0.text:
A Society convoy is {stopped on the hard shoulder|pulled up on the hard shoulder} with hazards going: four lorries, and the second one has its bonnet up and a driver underneath it who has been under it a while.
The rest are not helping. They are standing in a line facing back down the road, {watching the way they came|watching the road they came in on}.

choices.text: Ask what they are watching for.
Look in the second lorry's trailer.

a.text:
The fault is not a fault. {Somebody|Someone} has fitted a governor to the fuel line of the one lorry in the convoy carrying the one load that has to stay above eighty, and fitted it well.
Cutting it out takes an hour with {tool} and leaves the party's hands black to the wrist.

b.text:
They are watching for the car that passed them {twice|two separate times} in eleven minutes on a road with no turnings.
It is a Collective car, and it is not in a hurry, and the drivers have a rule about what happens on the third pass that they say out loud only once.

choices.text: Talk them out of the rule.

c.text:
{The trailer is water|What is in the trailer is water}: pallets of it, sealed, and the seals are Collective seals with the batch numbers filed off and a Society stamp put on over the top.
One pallet is open, one bottle is missing, and the driver under the bonnet has a bottle in his cab that he {has not opened and will not throw away|will neither open nor throw away}.

b1.text: The third pass comes {at dusk|at last light|as the light goes} with the lights off, and the road becomes, for {about|something like|roughly} ninety seconds, a thing that is happening rather than a thing anybody is on.

b2.text:
Talking four drivers out of a rule takes longer than the rule would have taken, and the argument is won on the point that the car has a plate and the plate can be written down and given to {somebody|someone} who bills by the letter.
The convoy rolls at midnight. The car does not make a third pass, and {somebody|someone} in an office is going to have a difficult quarter.

e_road_eighty.title: {Ninety on the Straight|The Rule of Eighty|The Car That Does Not Slow}

n0.text:
A car comes past the party on the straight doing {a good deal|a great deal|rather a lot} more than eighty, and there is a bubble marked on the map two miles ahead of it, and the driver knows this, because the map is the one printed by the county and everybody has it.
A hundred yards further on there is {vehicle} pulled over with a woman beside it who has been trying to flag the car down for a quarter of an hour.

choices.text: Ask the woman what she knows.
Go up the road after the car.
Look at the bubble edge itself.

a.text:
What she knows is that it is the fourth time this week, {always the same car, always the same time|the same car, at the same time, every time}, and that it goes in and does not come out and is back on this straight the following morning.
{She has stopped trying to warn the driver.|She has given up trying to warn the driver.} She is here to find out who is putting the car back.

b.text:
Two miles up the road there is no wreck, no car, and no bubble edge that anybody could point at, and the tarmac is warm in a strip {about|something like|roughly} as wide as a car.
At the far end of the warm strip {somebody|someone} has left {relicWord} on the verge, squarely, as though for collection.

c.text:
The edge, close up, is a disagreement in the air about a hand's breadth thick, and things put through it slowly come back and things put through it fast do not.
{tool} goes in at walking pace and comes back. Thrown hard, it does not, and something the same weight and the wrong shape arrives at the party's feet instead.

a1.text:
At six {in the morning|first thing|before noon} the car comes back out of the bubble at ninety, going the other way, with {nobody|no one} in it, and parks itself on the straight where it always parks.
What is in the boot is what {somebody|someone} has been posting into a time loop for {few} days, and it is addressed to a name in {country} that the party will now have to decide what to do with.

a2.text:
{She does not go home|She will not go home}, but she does move her vehicle out of the road, which is what the party actually meant.
What she gives them for the advice {is her father's|was her father's}, off the seat, and she is glad enough to be rid of it that the party does not argue.

e_ocean_fisher.title: {The Boat With No Name|Fishing the Wrong Water|One Line Out}

n0.text:
There is a boat sitting where there is no bank, no shelf and no reason to sit, with one line out and {stranger} on the tiller who has been there long enough to be sunburnt on one side.
{The catch box is full.|The catch box is full to the lid.} What is in it did not come out of this water, and everybody involved knows it.

choices.text: Ask what is on the end of the line.

a.text:
The box holds fish that are wrong in the small ways: a fin too many, a colour that belongs {three thousand|two thousand|four thousand} miles south, one with a ring through its lip that has a date on it {few} years from now.
They are all, without exception, in excellent condition, and the man will trade the whole box for something that floats better than what he has.

b.text:
On the end of the line, {sixty|forty|eighty} fathoms down, is something with weight and patience that has been on it since morning, and he has not tried to bring it up because bringing it up is the party's decision now.
He hands the rod over {the way a man hands over a dog he is fond of|the way you hand over a dog you are fond of}.

c.text: A line put in alongside is taken within a minute, {and then|then|and after that} again, {and then|then|and after that} a third time, and the man says this is the water doing what it does when {somebody|someone} new is over it.

e_lake_angler.title: {The Angler at the Sluice|Nothing Has Been Caught Here Since {timeAgo}|The Still Water}

n0.text:
The lake has not got a ripple on it and there is an angler on the sluice who says nothing has been caught here since {timeAgo}, and that he comes {every day|day in and day out}.
He is not lying about either. His keepnet is full and he has not caught any of it.

choices.text: Ask where the net came from.
Walk round to the sluice gear.

a.text:
The net fills overnight, every night, and has done since the water went still, and he has stopped telling people because of the two who came to look and the one who is still coming.
He would like {somebody|someone} to be here {at dawn|at first light} who is not him.

b.text: The water takes the bait the moment it lands, every time, and gives nothing back, and the {fifth|sixth|fourth} cast is the one that goes properly wrong.

c.text:
The sluice gear has been wound shut and welded, and the weld is old, and the plate over it carries {sign} and a date and an office in {country} that closed in the eighties.
What is behind the gate is not water. What comes out of the seam, slowly, all day, is.

e_beach_surf.title: {The Set Nobody Rides|Out Past the Point|Six Waves}

n0.text:
Round the point there is a set running that has no business running on this coast: {six|seven|five} waves, evenly spaced, breaking left, all day, on a beach with no swell.
There are boards stacked against the sea wall, waxed and dry, and {nobody|no one} in the water, and a man watching who nods at the party as though they are expected.

a.text: The water is warmer than the air and the set is {exactly|precisely} as regular from inside it as it looked from the wall, which is {the part that gets under the skin|what gets under the skin}.

b.text:
{Nobody|No one} is in because the set started {timeAgo} on the day the local lad went out and did not come back, and it has not missed an hour since, and the town has decided what that means.
The man watching is his father. He waxes the boards every morning. He would take it kindly if {somebody|someone} rode it who did not know the boy.

c.text:
The tideline has the usual: rope, plastic, a shoe. It also has a line of objects placed above the wrack in a row a hundred yards long, none of them wet, all of them from the same wreck.
The wreck is not on any list. The objects have been arranged by {somebody|someone} with time, at low water, {every day|day in and day out}.

n0.text:
Berth {few} is loading water: pallets of it, sealed, Collective seals, going out on a coaster with a manifest that says fertiliser.
The crane driver has been asked to keep the boom over pallet {few} hundred for the last twenty minutes and has not been told why, and neither has the checker, who has stopped checking.

a.text:
Pallet {few} hundred is not water. It is water bottles full of something the colour of water that separates when it stands, and there are {ninety|eighty|a hundred} of them, and one is missing.
The missing one is on the quay office desk, half drunk, next to a man who is not going to finish his shift.

choices.text: Take the pallet's paperwork and go.

b.text:
The checker has been a checker for {lots} years and has never once been told to stop checking, and he is taking it personally {in the manner of|in the way of|the way of} a man who has nothing else.
He gives the party his book. Every batch, every seal, every discrepancy, in pencil, going back {few} years, and the discrepancies are not random.

c.text:
The manifest is honest about everything except the one line that matters and dishonest about that in a way that requires a second manifest to exist somewhere.
The second manifest is in the coaster's chartroom, and the mate will sell it for {coin} {without being asked|unprompted|before anybody asks} {twice|two separate times}.

a1.text:
The doctor is {few} streets up and takes one look and asks, in the tone of a man who has asked before, which berth.
The man on the quay lives. The Collective withdraws the pallet, {quietly|without fuss}, and {somebody|someone} who has never met the party makes a note of them.

a2.text:
The paperwork on pallet {few} hundred names an office, a chemist, and a delivery address in {country} that is a school.
It is worth {a great deal|a good deal|rather a lot} to three separate parties, and the party has it, and the man on the quay does not get to a doctor.

e_fields_pigeon.title: {The Loft in the Middle of Nowhere|Ninety Miles an Hour With a Tailwind|Post}

n0.text:
In the corner of a field with nothing else in it there is {a pigeon loft on legs|a pigeon loft up on legs}, painted, maintained, and stocked, and a track worn to it from a road {half a mile|a mile|a quarter mile} off.
One bird is in and has been in a while, and it is carrying a stick of memory the size of a fingernail on a leg ring, and the loft's book has not been signed since Thursday.

choices.text: Sign the book and wait for whoever comes.

a.text:
The stick has {few} hours of {somebody|someone} talking on it, calmly, from inside a place where it is always the same day, describing what has changed since the last {few} hours.
Halfway through, the voice stops describing and starts asking whoever is listening to do one thing, and names a house in {country}.

choices.text: Send the bird back with an answer.

b.text:
Who comes is a girl of {about|something like|roughly} twelve on a bicycle who does the loft {twice|two separate times} a day for a man who cannot leave his farm, and who is {completely|utterly|altogether} unsurprised to find strangers at it.
She pays the party in {food} out of her saddlebag for having waited, which is the local rate for not stealing pigeons.

c.text:
The loft book goes back {many} years and it is a record of the edges of {few} separate bubbles moving, week by week, in the handwriting of six different people.
Whoever has been keeping it has been keeping it better than anybody official, and the last {few} pages are a map.

a1.text:
The house is shut up, the garden is nine months gone, and the one thing the voice asked for is {exactly|precisely} where the voice said, in a tin, under a slab, with a letter that has been rewritten {few} times.
Getting it back to the loft is a day's walk. Sending it in is a bird's five minutes.

a2.text:
An answer written on the back of {paper} and tied to a leg ring goes out over the field and is gone in {about|something like|roughly} {few} seconds.

p_oslo_mahyem.title: {Four Bars, Over and Over|The Rehearsal Room|Gods of a Cold Country}

p_napoli_camper.title: {The Yard on the Hill|Three Campers on Blocks|Somebody Else's Engine}

Fixing it is a day's work and a night's argument, and what is actually wrong with it is that {somebody|someone} removed one component before abandoning it, {deliberately|on purpose}, and took it with them.

a1.text:

p_taranto_launch.title: {Volunteers Free of Charge|The Armoured Rocket|Nine Out of Ten}

n0.text:

p_omega_lift.title: {The Goods Lift|Floor Nine Hundred and Something|Neutral Ground}

n0.text:

Inside, in wool, is a stone with a face on it that has come out of the White Desert, and it is a god that stopped being believed in, and {somebody|someone} has been shipping them up the Tower {one at a time|one crate at a time}.

p_milano_note.title: {The Strip in the Note|Counting Without Looking|The Man Who Is Not a Man Any More}

n0.text:
In the arcade there is a man counting notes without looking at them, {fast|at speed|quickly}, and getting it right, and he has been doing it for an hour {with the same bundle|on the same bundle}.

Take one note and look at the strip.

He is, he explains without stopping, performing a rite, and the rite is the same rite that deified a central banker, and it requires only two things: the name, and a great many repetitions of the name.

The bundle came out of a bank that failed in the spring and it should have been pulped and it was not, and the serial numbers run consecutively for {few} thousand notes.

The strip in the note has flecks in it that do not reflect anything, at any angle, and the note is warm where the strip runs, and the party is holding a piece of the outer wall of the Tower in their hand.

p_kola_shaft.title: {Twelve Kilometres Down|The Cap Is Welded|What Came Up in 1970}

n0.text:
The cap over the shaft is welded, bolted, and welded again, and there is a hut with a stove and two men who are paid to sit in it and listen.
What they are listening for comes up the shaft {about|something like|roughly} twice a week, faint, and on a rhythm, and they have been writing the rhythm down for {lots} years.

a.text:
The notes are neat, dated, and pointless for the first eleven years, {and then|then|and after that} a man called Vasiliev starts writing the rhythms in groups of four and the groups start repeating.
By the twentieth year it is unmistakably a language, and by the twenty-fifth {somebody|someone} has been answering it, and the answers are in the same book in a different hand.

b.text:
It comes at {few} {in the morning|first thing|before noon}, up twelve kilometres of hole, and it is not a machine noise and it is not water, and it stops the moment anybody in the hut speaks.
It starts again when they stop. It has done this for {lots} years and both men have long ago decided not to think about it in those terms.

c.text:
In 1970 the drill went {deeper than the drill should have gone|further down than any drill should have gone}, and what came up the shaft afterwards was not rock samples, and the surface has been dealing with the consequences ever since in {every country that has a coast|every country with a coast}.
The two men in the hut are the last of a programme that officially ended in the eighties, and they are still being paid, and neither of them knows by whom.

a1.text:
Whoever answered came up here four times in the nineties with {a translator's ear and no authorisation|a translator's ear and no permission at all}, and left, each time, by the shaft.
{The fourth entry in their hand is not an answer.|The last entry in their hand is not an answer.} It is a set of directions, downward, and the shaft cap has been opened and rewelded once since the last of them.

a2.text:
Answering it means striking the cap in groups of {few}, at {few} {in the morning|first thing|before noon}, in a rhythm the party has had {lots} years of notes to learn from a book.
What answers is closer than twelve kilometres, and it is coming up, and it is not in a hurry, and the two men in the hut go and stand outside.

x_vat_witch.title: {The Woman They Are Going to Burn|Umbra Excidii, Field Office|Arcane, in {country}}

n0.text:
In {power} territory there is {exactly|precisely} one legal way to be a mage and she is not it, and half the village {already|by now} knows, and the half that knows is the half that has been going to her at night with {misfortune}.
The party finds out the ordinary way: a boy of {about|something like|roughly} nine tells them, in the street, in daylight, because {nobody|no one} has explained to him yet that this is the kind of thing you get burnt for.

Ask the parish priest where he stands.

She is {lots}, sensible, and has a bag packed by the door that she has repacked {few} times this year, and she has known this was coming since the spring.
What she cannot do is walk out of a country that checks papers at every county line, and what she will not do is leave the {few} families who need her every week without telling them why.

b.text:
The field office is {two rooms over a bank|two rooms above a bank}, and the Umbra Excidii are three men and a woman who are all, without exception, arcane practitioners themselves, which is the arrangement: burn, or be recruited to find the others.

The priest has known for nine years and has been writing a letter to his bishop for six of them, and has not sent it, and shows the party the drafts.
He will not denounce her and he will not protect her, and he says both {plainly|flatly} and is ashamed of {exactly|precisely} one of them.

a1.text:
Getting her out is {few} county lines, a Society lorry, a set of papers that cost more than the lorry, and one checkpoint where everything depends on {leader} being {extremely|entirely|thoroughly} boring for ninety seconds.

a2.text:
A licence in this Empire means sacred or technomantic, and what she does is neither, and the only route through is to have her work reclassified by {somebody|someone} senior enough that {nobody|no one} will check.
It takes a month, {coin}, and a cardinal's secretary who owes {somebody|someone} a favour, and at the end of it she is legal, in writing, forever, in a country that burns people.

b1.text:
They write it down and thank the party without warmth, and they pay the standing rate, which is {generous|more than generous}, and they go that night.
They do not burn her. They recruit her, which is what they do with the ones who are any good, and in a year she will be the one at the door of {somebody|someone} else's kitchen with a name to write down.

b2.text:
Giving the Umbra Excidii a name that is not hers means giving them a name that is somebody's, and the party spends two days establishing that the {somebody|someone} is an office in the capital rather than a person.
It works for {about|something like|roughly} {many} days. What the party takes out of the field office in the meantime is the board itself, with {few} names on it, three of whom can now be warned.

n0.text:
The church has a {relicWord} that worked, reliably, within living memory, and stopped on the thirty-first of December and has not worked since, and the parish has been told to {keep saying the words anyway|say the words anyway}.

Talk to the man from the diocese.
Ask what it used to do.

b.text:
The man from the diocese is a canon lawyer, is exhausted, and is the fourth one sent to a parish like this in {a month|four weeks}, and he shows the party the schedule.
Every sacred object in the province is being collected because none of them work any more, and the Empire has decided that a hundred thousand people finding that out {at once|all at the same time|together} is worse than a hundred thousand crates.

It cured the thing it cured, in this valley, four or five times a year, for {two hundred|three hundred} years, and the register is in the sacristy and is not vague.

Making it work again is a mini rite: one artifact instead of seven, one night instead of {the whole of|all of} one, and the caster taking the risk of losing the memories or worse.

Talking {lots} people out of a locked church takes until two {in the morning|first thing|before noon} and the argument that wins is not the theological one, it is the one about what happens to the parish when the diocese sends {somebody|someone} who is not a canon lawyer.

x_brit_archive.title: {The Black Archive|Six, and the Other Six|A Reading Room With No Catalogue}

n0.text:

Whoever she is expecting is here to take one item out under a warrant, and she produces the warrant, and it is signed by an office that has not existed since {the Falklands|the Falklands war}.
She knows this. She has known for {few} days. She has been waiting to see whether the person who came for it would notice.

The room holds everything Britannia took out of circulation about a certain spell and a certain war, and there is no catalogue, {on purpose|deliberately}, and the order of the shelves is the catalogue.
She will not let the party read. She will let them look at the order of the shelves, which for a reader of her quality is a considerable gift and she knows it.

c.text:
Two Foundation archivists came on {Monday|Tuesday|the Monday} with a publication order and were shown the door, and one of them came back on Tuesday alone and was not shown the door, and did not leave for {six|five|seven} hours.

Noticing out loud gets the party {the whole of|all of} it: the warrant, the office, the {few} items that have gone out on it since {timeAgo}, and the fact that she has been logging every one and telling {nobody|no one}.
What she gives them to carry out is not from the shelves. It is her log, and she would like it to exist somewhere that is not this building.

a2.text:
The item is a wax cylinder in a tin, and it comes off the shelf without ceremony, and the party is {few} streets away before anybody works out that it is not going where the warrant said.
What is on it, played back, is {somebody|someone} being taught the pronunciation of a spell that took an Argentine fleet apart, one syllable at a time, {patiently|without hurry}.

x_ussr_deep.title: {The Listening Post|Deeper Than the Drill|Comrade, There Is Something Under the Floor}

n0.text:
There is a listening post on the ridge with a mast, a generator, and three people who are officially studying seismicity and are actually counting something coming up.
The count is chalked on the wall. It was {few} a month in the seventies. It was {few} a week in the nineties. It is {few} a day now, and they have stopped chalking it.

a.text:
Movements, they say, which is the word in the reports, {and then|then|and after that}, after {drink}, they say what the word means: something is going up and down a shaft system under half a continent, on a schedule.
The schedule is the interesting part. It is not a machine's schedule. It is a shift pattern.

Ask what the surface is going to do about it.

b.text:
The equipment is {lots} years old, beautifully maintained, and has one instrument on it that came from a Guild workshop and is not on any inventory, and it is the only one that is not {lots} years old.
It reads something the others do not. What it reads is not seismic and the three of them have no idea what it is for.

c.text:
When it reaches {few} an hour, the standing order is to burn the post and walk west, and the order is dated 1971 and has never been revised.

The surface, they say, is going to do {exactly|precisely} what it did in 1970, which is dig, and there are two new boreholes funded this year in a country that cannot fund boreholes.

x_gob_metal.title: {Corpse Paint and Diplomacy|The Horde's Post Office|Four Gods From a Cold Country}

n0.text:
The Horde holds this ground and holds it the way a tide holds a beach, and there is a hut at the edge of it that is, in every practical sense, a post office: notices in, notices out, and a Naguka clerk who is {very|remarkably} proud of the job.

The notice is four sentences and three of them are threats and the fourth is a date, {and it is on Vatican paper|and it is written on Vatican paper}, from the mission, and it is the fourteenth of its kind.

n0.text:
